gap_map.why_it_matters: dotnet-test covers execution and testability but not selection. The judgment about which behavior earns a test stays uncovered.
.NET solutions accumulate projects. Nothing decides when a folder should become a project, or when a shared project has turned into a grab bag that every other project references.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor applies references/growth-signals.md with the stack thresholds below.

layers.name: unit
layers.belongs_here: individual components or methods - and, per Microsoft's own guidance, only code within the developer's control: unit tests do not test infrastructure concerns such as databases, file systems or network resources
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the test needs a database or a WebApplicationFactory to reach one assertion

layers.name: integration
layers.belongs_here: two or more components working together - and, again per Microsoft, these often do include infrastructure concerns
layers.cost: slower; needs real or containerised dependencies

layers.name: functional (WebApplicationFactory)
layers.belongs_here: the real pipeline: middleware, model binding, filters, authorization and DI wiring
layers.cost: moderate, and it catches the mistakes unit tests structurally cannot see

layers.name: load
layers.belongs_here: whether the system handles a specified load - Microsoft lists this as a first-class test type
layers.cost: needs an environment resembling production to mean anything

testing.proportions: No proportions stated by Microsoft. Their definition sets the boundary instead: unit tests do not touch infrastructure, integration tests often do. That line decides where a test belongs more reliably than any ratio.
rules: A unit test that reaches a database, the file system or the network is an integration test that has been mislabelled - Microsoft's own definition draws that line.
Use WebApplicationFactory for integration tests over the real pipeline: it catches the middleware, authorization and DI mistakes unit tests cannot.
dotnet test runs every test project in the solution. Run it, not a filtered subset, before reporting a task complete.
Pick one test framework per solution. MSTest, NUnit, TUnit and xUnit are all supported; mixing them doubles the conventions a contributor must know.
traps: Async tests returning void instead of Task: exceptions are swallowed and the test passes regardless of what happened.
An in-memory EF Core provider accepts queries and constraint violations that a real database rejects, so the suite is green and the deployment is not.
A shared WebApplicationFactory carries state between tests, so a test passes alone and fails in the suite - or the reverse.
Static state and singletons persist across tests in the same assembly; test order then changes the result.
Mocking DbContext produces a test that asserts the mock's behaviour rather than any query the database would run.
what_not_to_test: Auto-properties, constructors and pass-through methods with no branching.
Framework behaviour: that model binding bound, that the DI container resolved.
EF Core migration classes themselves; assert on the resulting schema.
testing.notes: WebApplicationFactory gives real integration tests over the actual pipeline, which catches the middleware and DI mistakes that unit tests structurally cannot see.

growth_thresholds.extract_service_layer: an endpoint or action method exceeds 30 lines
growth_thresholds.extract_project: >=2 projects reference the same internal folder by relative path

architecture.pattern: layered solution with projects as the boundary

layers.name: Web / API project
layers.holds: endpoints, middleware, model binding, the composition root where DI is configured
layers.must_not: business rules - an action method past ~30 lines has absorbed the service

layers.name: Application / service layer
layers.holds: business rules and use cases, callable without HttpContext
layers.must_not: knowledge of the transport or of EF Core specifics

layers.name: Infrastructure
layers.holds: EF Core, external services, file and network access
layers.must_not: business policy - it implements interfaces the layers above define

variants.name: Single project
variants.cost: nothing enforces the layer boundary but review; it erodes quietly

variants.name: Layered projects in one solution
variants.use_when: the common shape: Web, Application, Infrastructure, and Domain if the rules justify it
variants.cost: project references must be maintained, and a wrong one is how Infrastructure ends up referenced by Domain

variants.name: Vertical slices
variants.use_when: features are independent and each owns its request, handler and data access end to end
variants.cost: cross-cutting concerns get duplicated per slice unless deliberately shared

rules: Project references are the architecture. Web references Application, Application references Domain, Infrastructure implements interfaces defined above it - and Domain references nothing.
An action or endpoint translates HTTP and delegates. Business rules go where they can be tested without a WebApplicationFactory.
The composition root is the Web project. Nothing below it constructs its own dependencies.
Every new endpoint states its authorization decision explicitly, including [AllowAnonymous] on purpose.
Never let EF Core types leak past Infrastructure: an IQueryable returned upward makes the database schema part of every caller's contract.
architecture.component_library: Not applicable. Promote shared code to its own project at >=2 consuming projects; below that, a folder is enough.
architecture.notes: Microsoft publishes several reference architectures rather than one mandate. What is not negotiable in any of them is the direction of project references, which is why the rules focus there.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Both are first-class in ASP.NET Core and they organise, test and version differently.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Minimal APIs for small surfaces; controllers when filters, conventions and model binding attributes are doing real work.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Mixing them without a rule means two places to enforce authorization and two conventions for every contributor.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Microsoft documents two platforms - VSTest and Microsoft.Testing.Platform - and four frameworks. Nothing picks for you.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: One per solution, chosen once. All four are supported; consistency is what matters.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A solution with two frameworks needs two sets of conventions, two runners and two CI configurations.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: EF Core, Dapper and ADO.NET are all supported and shape the code above them differently.
options: EF Core plus Dapper for hot paths
key_decisions.reasonable_default: EF Core unless the queries are the product.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: EF Core's change tracking and lazy loading leak upward, so replacing it later is not a swap.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: A solution can be one project or ten, and project references are what actually enforce the architecture.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Single project until a boundary is real; then layered, with references pointing one way only.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A reference added in the wrong direction is trivial to add and expensive to remove once code depends on it.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Available features and startup behaviour differ between a long-lived host and a serverless one.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Background services and in-process caches that work under a long-lived host silently do nothing under serverless.

operability.observability: ILogger with structured logging, and OpenTelemetry for traces and metrics. Exception handling middleware is where an unhandled exception becomes a recorded, shaped problem response instead of a bare 500.
operability.authorization: Authorization policies. Set a default policy so endpoints must opt out with [AllowAnonymous] - then an unmarked endpoint is protected rather than public.
done_checks: the app starts with the production configuration
clean clone and build from scratch
rules: Register HttpClient through IHttpClientFactory with an explicit timeout. A raw HttpClient with the default timeout and no policy exhausts sockets and waits far too long.
Set a default authorization policy so a forgotten attribute fails closed instead of open.
Exception handling middleware reports unhandled exceptions. Without it they become 500s with no record.
Configuration is validated at startup with options validation, so a missing value fails the deploy rather than the first request.
EF Core migrations are applied deliberately, never automatically at startup in production - an automatic migration on a rolling deploy runs from several instances at once.

dead_code_risks: Types resolved from the DI container by interface rather than by direct construction
Controllers and endpoints reachable only through routing
Types instantiated by reflection, including serialization targets and source-generated code
EF Core migration classes discovered by assembly scan
public members of a class library consumed by another solution
Code behind a feature flag that is currently off
